<reason>CON (Side A) won by narrowing the debate to a single decisive question—whether abolition changes anything other than screening intensity—and holding that ground through every round. CON's "end, not fix" frame, the residency/citizenship distinction, and the "other doors" argument survived the exchange: PRO's Caribbean-passports-don't-open-Vienna claim was factually shaky and CON corrected it; PRO's answer to the residency-only challenge was an explicit "I can't," followed by a "silence proves danger" move that CON fairly labelled unfalsifiable. PRO's best material—the seller-as-gatekeeper conflict of interest and the "product vs discretionary immigration law" distinction—was genuinely strong, and the closing's reframing of "zero marginal exposure" as an admission was rhetorically deft. But CON's closing answered it directly (same arrivals, less scrutiny; EU-level oversight is the reform PRO's own evidence shows working on Malta). PRO also never adequately defended the housing plank after CON's rebuttal. Both sides used plausible background knowledge without fake sourcing; both were clipped at points. CON made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Q2 asking PRO to name one residency-only program that failed under external oversight, and CON's follow-up in Rebuttal 2 turning PRO's "I can't… silence proves light scrutiny" into an unfalsifiable standard, combined with the "same people, less scrutiny" framing that neutralized PRO's "zero marginal exposure" reversal.</best_rebuttal>
